sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent speech-to-speech models [12, 41] are able to model full-duplex voice interaction in real-time, paving the way for voice assistants that hold natural and smooth conversations. However, these models only generate audio signal. In contrast, human spoken communication relies on visual cues and facial expressions, via an interplay of the audio and visual modalities. For instance, lip motion alters perceived phonemes [36], visual cues sharpen comprehension in noise [47], and an embodied talking face enhances the sense of social presence over voice alone [6]. To model such behaviors, audio-driven video generation models can synthesize talking-head videos from reference image and an input speech audio, enabling applications such as virtual avatars, synthetic presenters, and non-player characters in games. All these applications, however, share common constraint: the avatar must be generated on-the-fly, as the audio arrives, from stream of audio of unbounded duration. State-of-the-art talking-head models such as TalkVerse [52] and Wan-S2V [17] produce high-quality audio-driven videos but are ill-suited to the streaming setting. Because they rely on bidirectional attention, they must generate entire video chunks of several seconds at once, running dozens of denoising steps over the full chunk before producing any frame, which on single GPU takes minutes per chunk. Recently, CausVid [59] and Self-Forcing [23] have explored distilling such bidirectional video diffusion teachers into few-step causal students that generate video chunk by chunk in an autoregressive manner. However, these methods target only the text-to-video and image-to-video settings. Extending this approach to the audio-driven setting, where the model must additionally track dense time-aligned speech signal, has so far been demonstrated only on much larger models (1418B parameters) [24, 33, 42], which remain too large for real-time inference on single GPU (only 2 fps). second obstacle is the scarcity of suitable training data: existing public talking-head datasets such as Hallo3 [9] and CelebV [63] consist of clips too short to cover the chunk length of modern teachers like TalkVerse, ruling them out for distillation (see Section 3.6). We introduce AURA, family of causal few-step speech-to-video (S2V) models that generate streaming talking-head videos from live audio. In particular, AURA 1.3B runs in real time, generating 576p video at 20.7 frames per second for 16 Hz playback rate on single GPU, which makes it directly usable for the interactive applications above, such as talking face for voice assistant. AURA 5B targets higher resolution: it streams 720p video at 9.7 fps, 17 speedup over its TalkVerse teacher. For training, we generate and release new talking-head dataset comprising 30K videos (38.7 hours) produced with TalkCOHEN ET AL.: AURA: AUDIO-DRIVEN STREAMING AVATAR Verse, conditioned on reference images and text descriptions from the Hallo3 dataset [9] and synthetic speech audio. To train our model, we use two-stage distillation pipeline, similar to CausVid: Stage 1 first trains the causal student to match the bidirectional TalkVerse teachers Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) trajectories in order to reduce the gap between the bidirectional teacher and the causal student architecture. Then, Stage 2 closes the few-step gap with Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) and backward simulation: by training the student on intermediate states from its own denoising rollouts, the Stage 2 loss reflects accumulating errors the student may actually produce at inference. To further improve efficiency, we train the model to support chunk-wise causal sliding window attention, allowing us to use rolling KV cache with bounded memory at inference. We also use single KV cache for all diffusion denoising timesteps, further reducing memory footprint. With this approach, on standard talking-avatar benchmarks, AURA 5B matches or improves on its bidirectional teacher on visual quality (FVD [50] and JEDi [34] metrics) and audio-visual alignment, while running 17 faster with only four denoising steps per chunk, and AURA 1.3B reaches comparable quality at lower resolution and in real time (23 faster than its own teacher). Both models are faster than all baselines we compare against in the same single-GPU setting. Figure 1 shows an excerpt of qualitative samples generated by both models, as well as their speedquality tradeoff against prior work. In summary, we introduce AURA, which makes the following contributions: two-stage distillation method (ODE-trajectory initialization followed by Distribution Matching Distillation with backward simulation) paired with streaming inference scheme based on rolling KV cache of past chunks, shared by both models; AURA 5B, causal few-step S2V model that matches or improves on its bidirectional teacher on FVD and JEDi metrics, with 17 speedup. Our inference pipeline streams 720p video at 9.7 fps on single GPU, the highest throughput among audio-driven baselines we compare against; AURA 1.3B, smaller model trained with the same pipeline, which streams 576p video in speedup real time on single GPU (20.7 fps generated for 16 Hz playback rate), 23 over its own bidirectional teacher; public dataset of 30K talking-head videos generated by TalkVerse from synthetic speech, released both as decoded videos and as the latent ODE trajectories of the teacher, to support future research on streaming S2V distillation, together with the weights of our 1.3B teacher and its own 30K ODE trajectories; live demo coupling AURA 1.3B with Unmute, cascaded voice assistant built on Kyutais streaming speech-to-text and text-to-speech models [60] and text LLM, in which users hold natural spoken conversation with synthetic avatar in real time on single H100 GPU, available at kyutai.org/aura.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Diffusion and Flow Matching. Image Generative models have evolved through several paradigms: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [4, 18, 25] are efficient as they generate images in single forward pass but suffer from known limitations around mode coverage and training stability. More recently, diffusion models [15, 20, 26, 40, 44, 45] and flow matching [30, 32] have become the dominant paradigm for image generation. Indeed, both 4 COHEN ET AL.: AURA: AUDIO-DRIVEN STREAMING AVATAR frameworks are closely related and model data through an iterative multi-step refinement process, yielding stable training with high sample diversity but at the cost of slow sampling. Most modern large-scale video generators, including our teacher TalkVerse [52], are trained under the flow matching framework, and our work also builds on this formulation. Video Diffusion Models. Recent work has further scaled diffusion for video generation. Early efforts such as Imagen Video [21], Make-A-Video [43], Align Your Latents [3], and Stable Video Diffusion [2] extended image diffusion to short clips, typically by inflating 2D architectures with temporal layers. More recent open-source and industrial models, Sora [5], Movie Gen [38], Open-Sora [62], CogVideoX [56], HunyuanVideo [27], and Wan [51] adopt diffusion transformer (DiT) architectures and operate in compressed latent space, scaling to 720p1080p resolutions and minute-long clips. These models are typically noncausal: they generate the entire video sequence jointly over 50 or more denoising steps, and are thus not well adapted to the latency requirements of streaming applications. Current SotA talking-head models are based on such architectures. For instance, Hallo3 [9] adapts CogVideoX [56] for portrait animation with DiT-adapted identity reference network, while closed-source systems such as OmniHuman [29] extend DiT-based audio-driven generation to full-body animation. In this work, we distill two such non-causal teachers built on Wan, TalkVerse [52] (from Wan2.2-5B) for AURA 5B and 1.3B teacher that we train from Wan2.1-1.3B for AURA 1.3B, into causal, few-step streaming students. Distillation of Diffusion Models. The slow inference of diffusion models has motivated extensive work on distillation, training faster few-step student to reproduce slow teachers output distribution. One particularly successful line is Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [58], which trains one-step student to minimize the reverse KL to the teacher via learned critic; DMD2 [57] extends it to few-step generator and introduces backward simulation, computing the loss on the students own rollouts rather than forward-diffused data. CausVid [59] applies DMD to distill non-causal video teacher into causal few-step student for streaming text-to-video. challenge specific to causal video distillation is the train/test gap: the student is trained on teacher-provided past frames but must condition on its own previously generated frames at inference. Self-Forcing [23] and its variants [10, 31, 54, 64] address this temporal gap by rolling the student out autoregressively through trainingtime KV cache with stop-gradient. We instead build on DMD2s backward simulation [57], which exposes the student to its own denoising trajectory, and adapt it to streaming video (Sec. 3.4) so that the student also conditions on its own past generations, without maintaining training-time cache. Streaming Talking Heads. handful of recent works tackle audio-driven talking-head generation in streaming and few-step setting. Talking Machines [33] is, to our knowledge, the first to address this regime, distilling 18B model with DMD and sparse causal attention; weights are not released. Live Avatar [24] distills the 14B Wan-S2V model [17] into 14B few-step student that runs at 16 fps and 480p on 5-GPU setup. SoulX-FlashTalk [42] adopts similar few-step distillation strategy from 14B teacher into 14B student and requires 4 GPUs to reach real-time throughput. In contrast, AURA streams on single GPU: AURA 5B distills 5B teacher into same-size causal 4-step student that delivers 720p video at 9.7 fps, and AURA 1.3B, trained with the same pipeline from our own 1.3B teacher, reaches real time at 576p (20.7 fps for 16 Hz playback rate). Closest to our work is Avatar Forcing [11] whose pre-print was concurrently published: It uses similar DMD-based distillation process but requires look-ahead window of future audio to generate each frame by design, leading to small yet incompressible streaming delay. sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: In this section, we present AURA, our two-stage pipeline that distills non-causal audiodriven video diffusion teacher (TalkVerse) into 4-step causal student. We first recall Distribution Matching Distillation (Sec. 3.1) and the TalkVerse teacher (Sec. 3.1) to introduce necessary notations and context. Section 3.2 then introduces the causal student and the perchunk mixed-timestep design that enables compact KV cache. Section 3.3 and Section 3.4 cover the two training stages, and Section 3.5 finally describes streaming inference.

sections.title: 3.1 Preliminaries
sections.content: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD). DMD [58] trains few-step student generator Gθ to match multi-step teacher diffusion model at the distribution level, rather than along individual sampling trajectories. Concretely, DMD minimizes, in expectation over the diffusion timestep (0, 1), the reverse KL divergence between the student distribution pgen and the data distribution pdata, both diffused to noise level t. We adopt [0, 1] throughout this paper, with = 0 corresponding to clean latents and = 1 to pure noise. While the densities pgen and pdata are intractable, the gradient of the KL with respect to θ admits closed-form expression as difference of two score functions evaluated on student samples: DMD Et θ (cid:2)θ KL(cid:0)pgen,t (cid:1)(cid:3) (cid:90) (cid:0)sdata(Ψ(Gθ (z),t),t) pdata,t Et sgen,η (Ψ(Gθ (z),t),t)(cid:1) dGθ (z) dθ dz, (1) where denotes the noise input to the student, Ψ( ,t) is the forward diffusion operator that produces sample at noise level t, sdata is the frozen teacher score, and sgen,η is an online score network (called critic in this paper) with parameters η that estimates log pgen,t on student samples. In practice, sgen,η is trained jointly with Gθ via the standard denoising score-matching loss on student samples, and the two are updated in an alternating fashion. Backward simulation. Directly applying DMD to multi-step students yields traininginference mismatch: at training time, the student is fed forward-diffused real samples xt = Ψ(x0,t), whereas at inference time, intermediate inputs come from previous denoising steps of the student itself. To close this gap, DMD2 [57] introduces backward simulation. At each training iteration, the student is unrolled for few denoising steps to produce synthetic intermediate sample ˆxt , which then replaces the forward-diffused real sample as input to the DMD objective. Because Gθ is itself few-step generator, this unrolling is cheap. The DMD gradient and the score-matching update for sgen,η are then computed at ˆxt rather than at Ψ(x0,t), aligning the input distribution seen during training with the one produced at inference. DMD2 also adds GAN loss on real data. We adopt backward simulation, together with the two time-scale update rule of DMD2, in the second stage of our pipeline (Sec. 3.4), but not the GAN loss: it requires real videos and makes training less stable. The DMD objective alone already brings our student close to its teacher (Sec. 4.3). TalkVerse Architecture. We use TalkVerse [52] as our teacher model, 5B-parameter audio-driven video diffusion model built on the Wan2.2-5B [51] DiT backbone. Its video VAE uses compression factors (t, h, w) = (4, 16, 16), enabling efficient 720p generation. The model is conditioned on reference identity image, speech audio track encoded with Wav2Vec2 [1] and injected via cross-attention to temporally aligned visual tokens, and text COHEN ET AL.: AURA: AUDIO-DRIVEN STREAMING AVATAR prompt encoded with T5-XXL [39]. Long videos are generated with sliding-window mechanism that conditions each window on set of motion frames compressed by FramePack module [61], and the reference image is assigned positional offset placed ahead of the denoised window. Inference uses 50 denoising steps with flow-matching solver and classifierfree guidance. We provide more detailed description in the supplementary material A.1. sections.content: To turn the 50-step bidirectional teacher (TalkVerse) into 4-step causal student, we introduce three architectural modifications: chunked causal sliding window attention, removal of motion frames, and per-chunk mixed timesteps. In combination, these changes also enable us to keep compact rolling KV cache as illustrated in Figure 2b. 0.64 at the 25 Hz native rate), whereas the teacher generates 30 latent frames ( Chunked causal attention. The student generates videos in chunks of nc = 4 latent frames ( 5 s) in single pass. We enforce causality between chunks in the student: during training, blockwise causal attention mask prevents frames in chunk Ci from attending to frames in chunks for > i, while attention is bidirectional within chunk (Figure 2a). No motion frames. TalkVerse normally conditions each generated video sequence on window of past frames (motion frames) to maintain temporal coherence across windows. In our causal student, the KV cache already carries the past context required for coherence, thus we remove the motion frame mechanism entirely. This also saves us the cost of few forward passes through the model required to process motion frames for every new chunk. Per-chunk mixed timesteps: compact KV cache. To avoid this, we train the model to handle sequences in which different chunks are at different noise levels: each chunk is assigned single diffusion timestep ti, shared by all frames within the chunk (Figure 3, center). This per-chunk mixed timesteps scheme follows CausVid [59], which adopts it without explicit motivation. We argue it is key design choice to enable compact streaming KV cache. At inference, the current chunk is fed at high noise level tcurr while previously generated chunks, cached in the KV cache, are at the lowest noise level reached during their own generation. The cache therefore stores keys and values at single low noise level per past chunk, rather than at every diffusion step (Fig. 2b). In contrast, prior streaming audio-driven models that retain multiple noise levels in the cache pay proportional memory cost [24].

sections.title: 3.5 Inference: Causal Generation with rolling KV Cache
sections.content: At inference, the student generates the video autoregressively, one chunk of 4 latent frames at time, in 4 diffusion steps per chunk. Within each chunk, we adopt the predict-and-renoise scheme of DMD2 [57] (see supplementary material A.2). To extend generation to longer sequences, we use rolling KV cache with first-chunk anchor that provides temporal context across chunks, and RoPE [46] re-indexing scheme that bridges training and inference. Rolling KV cache. The sampling scheme of DMD2 describes the denoising of single chunk. To generate longer videos, each new chunk must attend to previously generated chunks for temporal coherence. naive KV cache that stores keys and values for all previously generated chunks would grow linearly with video length. We instead use rolling cache of fixed size matching our sliding window attention training: 1. the first chunk is kept as fixed anchor that subsequent chunks always attend to. This mirrors the attention sink mechanism used to stabilize streaming language models [53] and also often adopted for streaming long-video generation [31]; 2. the latest chunks (n = 1 in our setting), which provide the immediate temporal context for local motion continuity. We keep single past chunk (n = 1): enlarging the window to = 2 does not improve quality overall while increasing cache size and lowering throughput (supplementary material, Table 11). All other chunks are evicted from the cache once they fall outside this window, which yields constant inference memory regardless of video duration. Moreover, thanks to the per-chunk mixed-timestep training described in Section 3.2, cached entries only need to store keys and values at the lowest noise level reached at the last denoising step of the chunk, rather than at every diffusion step. The same attention pattern is reproduced at training time by the blockcausal mask (Figure 2a), in single forward pass and without maintaining KV cache. RoPE indexing. At inference, generated-frame positions grow without bound, while the reference frame is anchored at fixed temporal RoPE position 10 to 40 latents ahead of the current generation front at training time (Section 3.1 and supplementary material A.1). To preserve this training-time configuration, we explore scheme to re-index the reference every 30 new generated latent frames, in the spirit of the re-indexed reference or sink frames of recent streaming avatar models [11, 24, 28], shifting it by +30 each time so that its offset relative to the generation front cycles between +40 and +10 (Figure 8 in supplementary material). This keeps the relative position of the reference within the regime the model was trained on, and avoids the position drift that would otherwise accumulate over long autoregressive rollouts. In practice, we find that this reindexing design helps stabilizing long generation for AURA 5B. For the smaller AURA 1.3B however, it is more beneficial to directly cap the RoPE positions of the generated frames to the range seen in training in our experiments, as Anchor Forcing [55] and StreamAvatar [48] do (supplementary material A.4).

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Architecture and initialization. We train two students with the same recipe, building on the open-source TalkVerse codebase for training and inference. AURA 5B is initialized from its teacher, TalkVerse [52] (5B parameters, built on Wan2.2 5B). AURA 1.3B is initialized from 1.3B bidirectional speech-to-video teacher that we train ourselves with the TalkVerse training pipeline, adapting Wan2.1 1.3B text-to-video [51] to speech as TalkVerse does from Wan2.2 5B, with LoRA adapters on the backbone and audio cross-attention layers. This teacher differs from TalkVerse in two ways. It is trained on much less data: 31 of real Hallo3 video (23K clips), whereas TalkVerse is trained for about one epoch on its 6.3K-hour dataset. Its audio features come from the Mimi speech codec [12] instead of Wav2Vec2: Mimi is more recent codec with causal, streaming encoder, and we keep its first, semantic level (Sec. A.4 of the supplementary material). Both students are trained with LoRA adapters [22] of rank 128 on the attention layers. We additionally unfreeze their timestep embedding and output head, since our models use the per-chunk mixed-timestep scheme of Section 3.2 rather than the single shared timestep of the teachers. Both generate video in chunks of nc = 4 latent frames with 4 diffusion denoising steps per chunk. They differ in output resolution and rate: AURA 5B generates 720p video (1216 960, depending on the aspect ratio of the reference) played back at 25 Hz, the native output rate of TalkVerse, and AURA 1.3B generates 576p video (768 576, likewise) played back at 16 Hz, the native rate of Wan2.1; we use fps (frames per second) elsewhere to denote throughput. Unless stated otherwise, experiments use AURA 5B. 768 or 960 512 or 576 COHEN ET AL.: AURA: AUDIO-DRIVEN STREAMING AVATAR 11 Two-stage LoRA training. Each stage trains its own LoRA adapters. At the end of Stage 1 (ODE teacher forcing), its LoRA is merged into the base weights, and Stage 2 (DMD with backward simulation) trains fresh LoRA of the same rank, avoiding stacked adapters. The Stage 2 critic is initialized from the teacher, and only its LoRA adapters are trained. Both models use batch size 256 and 5 critic updates per student update. AURA 5B runs Stage 1 for 120K steps at learning rate 1e-5 and Stage 2 for 5K steps at 3.5e-7, on 64 H100 GPUs. AURA 1.3B runs Stage 1 for 40K steps at 1e-5, on trajectories of its own teacher, and Stage 2 for 6.5K steps at 2e-7, on 32 H100 GPUs. Other hyperparameters, including the 1.3B teachers, are in the supplementary material (Sec. A.3, A.4). Baselines. We compare AURA against four open-source audio-driven avatar generation models. TalkVerse [52] , our teacher, serves as high-quality reference for the distillation. Wan-S2V 14B [17] and Hallo3 [9] are two recent large-scale non-causal S2V model. Live Avatar [24] is streaming few-step approach and the closest competitor to AURA in inference regime. For all baselines we use the authors released code and checkpoints, and run inference under each methods recommended settings. Benchmarks. We evaluate on two test sets we generate. HALLO3 TEST consists of 100 first frames and prompts randomly sampled from the Hallo3 test set [9], each re-paired with real English speech track from an internal dataset to assess speaker generalization; all clips are 10 s. CELEBV-HQ TEST consists of 150 first frames from CelebV-HQ [63], each paired with 820 of TTS-synthesized speech (same pipeline as Sec. 3.6) and the generic prompt person is talking; we synthesize rather than reuse audio because CelebV-HQ clips are too short ( Metrics. We evaluate along five axes. Visual quality: FID [19], FVD [50] on 16-frame windows, computed at three temporal offsets, @0 (initialization), @101 and @109 (windows centered on and starting at mid-video chunk boundary, capturing inter-chunk discontinuities), and JEDi [34], an MMD-based distance on V-JEPA features more reliable at our limited sample counts, at the same offsets. The main tables report the mean over the three offsets, and the per-offset values are in the supplementary material (Sec. A.5). (The 16-frame windows span 1 at 16 Hz and 0.64 at 25 Hz, so FVD and JEDi are only approximately comparable across output rates.) Temporal consistency: the warping error (WE), the mean L1 residual after RAFT [49] optical-flow alignment of consecutive frames, capturing flicker and chunk-boundary artifacts. Audiovisual alignment: Sync-C and Sync-D [8] (SyncNet). Identity preservation: CSIM, the mean cosine similarity between ArcFace [14] embeddings of the reference and generated frames. Inference timing: on single H100 GPU, 960 reference at each models generating one clip from fixed 10 English audio and 960 native resolution and frame rate; we report throughput (fps) for the DiT and VAE decoder separately and the end-to-end Total (excluding loading and warm-up). Total is not simple composition of the two: for Live Avatar, offloading the DiT or VAE between calls to fit in GPU memory adds overhead. 5 s) to test longer sequences.

Long-form streaming stability. central claim of AURA is that its rolling KV cache sustains generation over an unbounded stream at constant memory. To measure how quality and identity evolve over time, we run both models (4 steps) on the 100 HALLO3 TEST references driven by 60 of speech and compute metrics on consecutive 10 segments (Figure 7 and Table 10 in the supplementary material). For AURA 1.3B, FVD and lip-sync stay flat over the six segments (FVD 179186, Sync-C 4.734.81, no segment significantly different from the first), and so does identity for most videos (median per-video CSIM change 0.02 over the minute; few videos drift and pull the mean from 0.83 to 0.78). AURA 5B degrades slightly after the first segment (FVD from 182 to 195206, then stable) and its identity drifts slightly (CSIM from 0.76 to 0.69). Perceptual quality. Distribution-based metrics (FID, FVD, JEDi) capture global feature statistics but do not penalize certain local artifacts: Hallo3 obtains the best FID, FVD, and JEDi on both test sets, yet its generations exhibit exaggerated mouth motion and recurrent hand artifacts that these metrics fail to flag (qualitative analysis in Fig. 9, supplementary material). To assess perceived quality directly, we run an anonymous human evaluation on the Mabyduck platform. We collected 400 pairwise comparisons from 27 raters on the 100 HALLO3 TEST clips, covering all pairs among AURA 5B, AURA 1.3B, Hallo3 and our TalkVerse teacher, along four axes: overall visual quality, lip-sync, reference fidelity, and naturalness. Results are aggregated into per-axis Bayesian Elo scores  (Fig. 4)  . Both AURA models are preferred over Hallo3 on all four axes, confirming that Hallo3s distributionmetric lead does not translate into perceived quality. Against the non-causal 50-step teacher, AURA 5B ranks higher on reference fidelity, consistent with our CSIM results, and is on par on visual quality, lip-sync and naturalness, despite being causal and faster. AURA 1.3B also ranks above TalkVerse on reference fidelity, but below AURA 5B and TalkVerse on visual quality, which reflects its lower resolution, as well as on lip-sync and naturalness.

sections.title: 4.4 Qualitative Results
sections.content: Figures 1 and 5 show representative AURA generations, from both models, on different test sequences spanning varied lighting conditions, head poses, and identities. The generated frames remain faithful to the reference identity throughout the sequence, and exhibit natural motion patterns including spontaneous eye blinks, subtle head movements, and small facial expression variations that go beyond strict lip motion. Figure 10 in supplementary material compares AURA 5B to its TalkVerse teacher on the same input. Despite using only 4 denoising steps instead of 50, AURA matches the teachers visual quality, and in some cases improves over it: in the example shown, the TalkVerse output produces static gaze with no blinking over the full 10 clip, whereas AURA generates natural eye blinks and more varied global motion. Full videos for all sequences, including AURA 1.3B samples, are on the project page at https://kyutai.org/aura/.

sections.title: 5 Conclusions
sections.content: We present AURA, family of causal few-step speech-to-video models for streaming talkinghead generation. Distilling bidirectional teacher into same-size 4-step causal student through two-stage pipeline and rolling KV cache, AURA 5B matches or improves on its TalkVerse teacher on FVD and JEDi at 17 speedup, delivering 720p video at 9.7 fps on single GPU. AURA 1.3B, distilled with the same pipeline from 1.3B teacher, streams 576p video in real time on single GPU (20.7 fps for 16 Hz playback rate). We also release 30,000-clip synthetic dataset with teacher ODE trajectories, as well as our 1.3B teacher and its ODE trajectories, to support future work on audio-driven distillation. sections.content: A.1 TalkVerse We use TalkVerse [52] as the teacher of AURA 5B, 5B-parameter audio-driven video generation model built on the Wan2.2-5B [51] Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone, originally pretrained for text-and-image-to-video generation. TalkVerse extends the Wan-S2V [17] design for speech-conditioned video synthesis to the Wan2.2 backbone, and trades the 14Bparameter scale of Wan-S2V for smaller 5B model, trained on high-resolution opensource dataset. Latent space. TalkVerse uses the Wan2.2 video VAE, which downsamples by (t, h, w) = (4, 16, 16), higher compression ratio than the (4, 8, 8) commonly used in prior video diffusion models (e.g. Wan2.1). This yields 4 reduction in latent token count at the same resolution, enabling efficient high-resolution (720p) generation. Conditioning. The model is conditioned on three inputs: (i) reference identity image, (ii) speech audio track, and (iii) text prompt describing the video content. Audio is encoded with Wav2Vec2 [1] and injected into subset of DiT blocks via cross-attention from visual tokens to audio tokens, with each latent frame attending to temporally aligned audio segment. The text prompt is encoded with T5-XXL [39] and injected through crossattention. TalkVerse is trained on the large-scale TalkVerse-2.3M dataset of high-resolution audio-synchronized clips. Long-video generation: temporal context. To generate minute-long videos, TalkVerse uses sliding-window mechanism: each window denoises fixed number of frames conditioned on window of preceding frames, referred to as motion frames. To keep the token budget tractable, the motion frames are compressed by FramePack module [61] and assigned negative positional embeddings to mark them as past context. Long-video generation: reference frame placement. The reference identity image is assigned positional embedding placed after the denoised video window, specifically position 40 for denoised window of 30 latent frames. This forward offset makes the model chase the reference rather than copy it, which the authors report avoids copy-paste artifacts and looped body movements when the same reference is reused across sliding windows. Training and inference. TalkVerse is trained with LoRA on the DiT attention layers, while audio projection, audio cross-attention, and FramePack-related modules are fully fine-tuned. Inference uses 50 denoising steps with flow-matching solver and classifier-free guidance.
